subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PENITENTIARY INMATES ACQUIRING RIGHT TO VOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court of Ontario has decided that prison inmates in Ontario are entitled to vote. The court ruled that a provision in the Ontario Elections Act that disenfranchises prisoners is contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The effect of this decision is that all inmates, including federal inmates, will be allowed to vote in provincial elections. The effect of this decision is that inmates such as Helmut Buxbaum, Colin Thatcher, and Clifford Olson will be allowed to vote and to participate in the democratic process. That would be unconscionable, Mr. Speaker.
A Canadian citizen who is incarcerated and deprived of his freedom for committing a crime should also forfeit his right to vote. The right to vote should belong only to those who are Canadian citizens and to those who have respect for the rule of law.
1 call on the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to request that the Attorney General for Ontario immediately appeal the decision. As well, I call on the Government to seek an amendment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to exclude inmates specifically from the franchise.

Mr. Speaker, in order to promote and encourage job creation, the Quebec Municipal Economic Development Board has been associated with many projects in the industrial zones and parks of Quebec City.
In 1986, this resulted in some $41 million of investment. In 1987, the value of projects in which OMDEQ was involved reached $62 million, an increase of over 50 per cent. In two years, more than 2,000 jobs were maintained or created.
This performance reflects the dynamism of Quebec enterprise, small and medium-sized companies working in the service and high-tech sectors.
For 1988, we expect nearly $100 million in industrial and commercial investment for Quebec City. That is encouraging, Mr. Speaker! The very healthy economic climate resulting from the policies of the Conservative Party in Quebec and throughout the country is certainly responsible.
Like Andre Joncas, the director of OMDEQ, I would like to thank all those investors for openly showing their confidence in the promising future of the province's second most important economic centre, Quebec City, the capital.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF LONG-TERM DISASTER ASSISTANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago the Government announced some ad hoc drought assistance for western cattlemen. Being ad hoc in nature, the program is being designed and implemented on the run. It is already experiencing administrative problems.
First, cattlemen will have to wait several weeks before they can even get application forms. This means that they will experience cash flow problems well before the Government will be ready to pay out the promised assistance.

July 20, 1988
There is concern because the assistance rates are based on geographic areas which are too large to reflect drought damage accurately. Farmers on one side of a road may get less assistance than their neighbours on the other side of the road, even though both are equally affected by the drought. Other similar problems are coming to light.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) would implement a long-term disaster assistance program as he promised he would do three years ago, farmers would not be faced with these administrative headaches. New Democrats call upon the Government to act now to develop a long-term disaster assistance program for Canadian farmers.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA STRIKE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bell Canada strike by some 19,000 members of the Communications and Electrical Workers of Canada has to be resolved. I have here a letter from the Government Relations Department of Bell Canada which reads in part:
Despite the general walkout, the company is making every effort to maintain reasonable service to its customers.
The company should tell that to the people of Elmvale Acres and Chapel Hill in my constituency where serious sabotage has taken place in the last 24 hours which has knocked out the phone services there. In fact the people there cannot even get access to emergency services in the event that they are required.
Phones are an essential service in Canada now and should not be disrupted by sabotage. I am led to believe that neither party is talking. There is no expression that the parties want to get together. They are both unwilling to make concessions on key issues.
I call upon those concerned to stop burning cables and to start talking like intelligent, mature, responsible people. I also call on the Government to be prepared to appoint a mediator within 24 hours if no progress is made on this issue.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF HIGHLAND FISHERIES PLANT IN GLACE BAY, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last weekend, Highland Fisheries Ltd., a subsidiary of Clearwater Fine Foods of Halifax, closed its processing plant in Glace Bay, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, throwing 310 people out of work in a town where there is already chronic unemployment.
The company closed this plant without proper reason and with a total disregard for the contributions the federal Government has made to the company and its predecessor in the last number of years. The manner in which this company has gone about this closure shows a total lack of corporate integrity and will not be forgotten by the workers.
In light of the closure, the responsibility now lies with the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon). He can, using the many tools at his disposal, encourage senior management of that particular plant to reassess this closure and to have a business plan put in place in order to make the plant operational. The community and the workers want this to take place. They want co-operation. They want employment. They want the Government of Canada to come in on their side and fight for their economic interest by having this plant reopened.

Mr. Speaker, the housing crisis in the greater Metropolitan Toronto region becomes more acute as each day passes. Families are having a very difficult time buying a home due to high costs. In fact the perception beginning to set in is that, if you do not already own a home, you never will unless you have solid financial resources.
As a Government we must ensure that affordable housing is available to all. Presently the Town of Vaughan is in the process of negotiating with the federal Government the purchase of a 107-acre property owned by Environment Canada. The Government should sell the land with the condition that the majority of the site be used for affordable housing.
I believe that all surplus federal land which is to be sold must have affordable housing as its main usage.

APARTHEID-TREATMENT OF BLACK AND WHITE SOUTH AFRICAN ATHLETES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1977 Gleneagles Agreement which Canada signed specifically requires the signatories to discourage participation by their nationals in events involving South African athletes, and to withhold support for organizations promoting such contact.

*

July 20, 1988

Tennis Canada, a federally funded organization, invited two white South Africans to participate in the Players Cup next month in Toronto. Meanwhile, Albert Ramovha, a black softball player from Soweto, sought a visa on his own to attend, as a mere spectator, a tournament in Saskatoon. What was the Government's response? It was to deny the black softball player a visa because he might be mistaken for an official of his virtually all-black softball association.
There was no mistake with the white South African tennis players, for they were treated differently, and the invitation by Tennis Canada was legitimized. Why? Because $815,000 in prizes available to the South African tennis players make them admissible as entrepreneurs.
That is a policy so inconsistent with the Gleneagles Agreement, a policy based upon the greater weight of private profit over professional principle, a policy so discriminatory as to proclaim the victory of hyprocrisy over commitment, a policy intolerable to all opponents of apartheid that it must be changed so that Canada lives up in full measure to its commitment under Gleneagles.

Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, during each fiscal year the Opposition in the House of Commons has a total of 25 days to bring forward items and
issues it feels should be debated. On March 4, 1988, I introduced the following motion for debate:
That this House recognizes the pivotal role that NATO continues to play in mutual security and defence and in furthering progress in arms control and disarmament and, therefore, reaffirms its commitment to continued Canadian participation in and active support for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization as a primary instrument of Canadian defence policy.
At the end of the day's debate a vote was taken on the motion. The NDP voted against it. We did not expect a Conservative Government to do the same thing, but every Conservative MP and cabinet Minister did vote against the motion. Only the Liberal Party voted for this reaffirmation of the NATO alliance. The Government had been strong in its rhetoric about NATO and then stood up in this House and voted against this reaffirmation on behalf of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks Revenue Canada officials in Edmonton announced their intention to assess selected Edmonton taxi firms for unemployment insurance contributions for taxi drivers, based upon existing federal tax jurisprudence. Such assessments will be retroactive to January 1, 1987.
Edmonton taxi brokers have expressed deep concern that the introduction of such unemployment insurance contribution assessments on a selective basis will create instability and, mostly, unfairness in the Edmonton taxi industry as drivers will move to unassessed taxi firms.
The taxi industry is an essential component of the Edmonton transportation network, especially now as Klondike Days, a major tourist attraction, start tomorrow in Edmonton.
I urge the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to introduce a UI premium contributions moratorium until all Edmonton taxi brokers have been assessed and properly notified of Revenue Canada's policy intentions in this regard.

subsubtopic: LAND CLAIMS-OBSERVANCE OF SASKATCHEWAN FORMULA ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Indian people from all over the country, and especially from Saskatchewan, are becoming increasingly frustrated with the Conservative Government.

July 20, 1988
Oral Questions
This week the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations is hosting a forum at the Beardy Reserve to express their outrage at the Government's failure to settle outstanding land claims. Once again I and the New Democratic Party join Saskatchewan Indians in demanding that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) honour the Saskatchewan Formula, an agreement which was signed 11 years ago.

By failing to commit itself to settling land claims quickly the Government is demonstrating its lack of commitment to the Indian people of this country. This country needs a New Democratic Party Government which will respect the rights of all its people.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CARGOES CARRIED IN FOREIGN REGISTERED SHIPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, marine shipping in Canada is subject to a set of regulations, and I have not been advised of any violation of these regulations by any vessel whatsoever. Considering the Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of State for Finance. It concerns the relative value of our dollar and the level of interest rates. Can the Minister tell Canadians how he feels about the constant increase in the value of the Canadian dollar?

July 20, 1988
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: EXCHANGE VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-INTEREST RATES- MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the value of the Canadian dollar is the result of the strength of the Canadian economy.

The strength of the Canadian economy largely accounts for the strength of our dollar. It has risen slightly in the last few weeks because of the intrinsic strength of the economy. Retail sales are up. Housing starts are strong. The expansion of credit in this country has been growing very strong in the last two months as well. Basically we have an economy in which the world has confidence.
Second, there has been some repositioning of monetary positions taken regarding the U.S. dollar with the co-operation of the United States Federal Reserve. In the sell-off of the U.S. dollar some of this value has been repositioned in the Canadian dollar which technically lifts our dollar to a slightly higher level.
More important, the Hon. Member asks about interest rates and their effect on the Canadian dollar. I think the Hon. Member should know that the spread now between Canadian interest rates and U.S. interest rates has narrowed significantly in the last three months. Therefore, the exchange rate presently for the Canadian dollar is in no way a function of the spread. If anything, the spreads are narrower. The result is a strong economy. The world is confident, and that is why our dollar is strong.

Fur Industry

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on this motion introduced by the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) on July 18. It deals with the vital role the fur industry plays in our traditional rural economy.
All Hon. Members recall the emergency debate that took place in the House on June 1. Members from all Parties spoke on the concerns we all had that the British House of Commons was currently considering legislation which would require fur products to be labelled clearly to restrain in effect and check retailers from selling furs from Canada and the public from purchasing them.

They, along with all Hon. Members, gave a clear and strong message to the British Parliament.
We all know that the British Government scrapped that Bill on June 18. All Members of the House were very pleased with the news. However, I, along with other Members, realized at the time that it was just a small victory in a very long and determined battle with a group that was intent on destroying an industry and a way of life for so many Canadians.
Today we have another threat to the livelihood of many Canadians connected with the fur industry. The European Economic Community has put forward a motion which, if approved, will have the effect of moving forward the same legislation which the British Government scrapped on June 18 concerning the tagging of Canadian pelts.
I would like to take a few moments to speak about the economic aspect of the fur trade for Canadians. The industry is worth approximately $600 million annually. There is a spinoff of $200 million for allied industries. For the last two to three years, Canadian fur exports totalled approximately $350
million annually, much of that going to the European market. To put those figures into perspective, 105,000 Canadians earn all or part of their income from the fur industry. Approximately 100,000 are trappers, half being aboriginal people. More than 80 per cent of the retail fur sales in Canada are made through privately owned, family run, one store businesses.
Above and beyond the economics of this issue, and even more important, are the social and cultural factors involved when considering the native people and our northern communities. As you well know, in December of 1986 the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development presented the House with The Fur Issue Report. The committee heard from many Canadians who depend directly on the fur trade. The report said that, for native people, trapping involves more than simply trying to earn cash income. It implies a unique social, spiritual and cultural relationship with the land and its resources. For northern communities, trapping and trade are the activities which hold the people together, creating a bond of belonging, and providing all of the inhabitants with a purpose. Those comments were echoed time and time again in our committee hearings.
May I remind my colleagues in the House that this is not the first time we have been charged with defending our fur industry. Both in 1979 and 1982 we considered the serious threat and implications of the anti-fur campaign with respect to the seal hunt. Then the European Community banned imports of seal pup pelts as a reaction to a lobbying campaign based on an emotional appeal which was very shallow in its facts. Through an effective use of the media, the animal rights movement was successful. The devastation caused by the collapse of our industry, especially in the Maritimes, is well recorded.
There are towns today which are economically ruined, where families have had to move or have been torn apart. An entire way of life was altered because we were unable to put an effective case forward for our seal hunt. The loss of that hunt and what it meant for thousands of Canadians can still be seen today in family break-ups, bankruptcies, needless suicides, alcoholism, the loss of individual self-worth, dignity, and sense of belonging. We cannot allow those tragedies to reoccur.
The impact of the animal rights campaigns and the anti-fur campaigns, particularly those in Europe, have been felt by many Canadians. Our Government, in partnership with the Canadian Fur Institute and other representatives of the industry, has taken steps to address these concerns. In the past decade we have become increasingly active in the conservation and management of our wildlife, in the development of humane trap testing and design, trapper education, and education of the public on the trapping advancements which have been made in Canada. However, it is evident from the ever-increasing and constant pressure being applied by the animal rights groups and anti-fur lobbyists in Europe on their elected members that our efforts are not being fully recognized or appreciated.
July 20, 1988

Succinctly put, the animal rights groups are unrealistic in their goals, and if those goals are met it will undoubtedly be extremely harmful to the many Canadians who depend on the fur industry for their livelihood. What the British and European Parliamentarians and public must recognize about our fur industry is that it is the responsible harvesting of a renewable resource.
I raise this issue today because I feel it is extremely important at this time to send a strong message to the European Parliaments and public. What those elected representatives are being told through the animal rights lobby groups are distortions and manipulation of fact. As they did with the pup seal issue, these interest groups have singled out Canada and our export industry as their initial target. The European public is being fed videos, billboards and posters filled with misinformation and half-truths.
The time has come for Canadian Parliamentarians to act together. I say to my colleagues that we must remain steadfast in our support for the fur industry, for trappers across our country, and for our native communities and peoples for whom the fur trade is an integral part of their lives.
Canada is in the forefront of humane trapping research. The Canadian Government and the fur industry have already committed over $8 million to scientific research programs. The results of this research in terms of improved humane trapping technology, including leghold systems, is extremely positive.
Meetings with officials from the Department of External Affairs, the Department of the Environment and the Department of Indian Affairs have been ongoing. There have been meetings with European officials to gather support for our position. I call on all Members in this House to join together in sending to the European Community members the strongest support possible for the 105,000 Canadians who are directly and indirectly employed in a vitally important industry.
I believe it is fitting to close with this final comment on how important this industry is to Canadians. I wish to draw into focus what this debate is all about. This reflects not necessarily on an economic industry or an export commodity, but on the sense of being, livelihood and way of life of individual Canadians. During our hearings a trapper came before us and this is what he had to say about trapping:
I have been a trapper all my life. 1 had a family, but I lost my wife. I am just
by myself now. I am 69 years old. 1 draw the old age pension and 1 am still
trapping. I have never been to school. I just live in the bush. All I know is how
to sign my name on a cheque. I cannot read one word, but I love the way 1 live.
That is what we are talking about, the livelihood of individuals, and it is being jeopardized. I want to thank my colleagues for the support they have given on an issue vital to all northern Canadian communities.

Mr. Speaker, I, along with the other members of my Party, wish to indicate to the House that we support both the thrust and objective of this
Fur Industry
government-sponsored notice of motion regarding the fur trapping industry in Canada. We in this Party believe that the wording could have been even stronger but, leaving that aside, we believe we must convey a message of opposition to the European Parliament with regard to the misguided and destructive proposal to label fur products imported into the European Economic Community. These labels would have no purpose other than to create, in the minds of some consumers, a false and completely wrongly-based sense of guilt.
1 regret that time allows for only one speaker from each Party because there are many other Members in my Party who would want to express their views on this important issue of the fur industry in Canada. The Member of Parliament for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins), who is in the House today, would certainly have spoken in his usual eloquent way. In fact, he has spoken on this issue. He has raised questions in the House and is giving leadership in his own constituency to those for whom the fur industry is important.
My friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-[DOT] Twillingate (Mr. Baker), would also have spoken. He would have told the House about the devastating effect the EEC ban on the seal trade has had on communities of which he is aware. The same could be said for the Member of Parliament for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). They would all have spoken from personal experience and with considerable emotion on this important issue.
A mammoth new volume entitled Wild Furbearer Management and Conservation has just been released. It was published by the Ontario Trappers Association under a licensing agreement with the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources. It is an important piece of work. It is a large volume and costly to purchase, but I hope that many libraries will be able to buy it in order that more Canadians can be well informed about the fur industry in Canada.
This volume quite correctly points out that the fur trade played an important part in the economic development of North America. However, more to the point of today's debate, the fur trade remains a dominant industry in the vast boreal forest of the Canadian sub-Arctic which is the largest region in Canada. I have the good fortune to represent a significant part of that important region in our great country.
Climatic conditions favour the production in this region of very high quality fur pelts. Trapping for these pelts is a means of wildlife harvesting. I cannot emphasize that too strongly. It is wildlife harvesting. This means harvesting a resource which is renewable. Trapping for these pelts means that those who engage in the industry must be very conservation-minded because conservation is an essential aspect of this activity.

July 20, 1988
Fur Industry
The vast boreal forest region of Canada does not lend itself to other kinds of industrial activity. For example, it is not well suited to large-scale agriculture. Although this region of which I speak is very well endowed with minerals, economically viable mineral deposits are found in only relatively small portions of that area. The forestry resource is substantial but commercial exploitation is generally restricted to the southern periphery of this region. Thus it is, Sir, that the fur trade is still the region's most extensive industry providing some income to the greatest number of people.
In Canada about 100,000 people are engaged in trapping. More than one-half of these are aboriginal trappers. We can safely estimate, given an average of four people in an aboriginal household, that nearly one-quarter of a million aboriginal people in Canada rely to some extent on the fur trade, a trade which in a good season may bring in between $5,000 and $10,000. That is not a great deal of money, but it is used to buy essential equipment manufactured elsewhere but needed in these modern times by our aboriginal people.
I say to you, Sir, and to all Members of the House, that if the fur industry collapses-and the proposal now before the European Parliament will, to a significant extent, contribute to that collapse if it happens-it is the aboriginal people of Canada who will suffer the most.
As many Members of Parliament know, the seal ban by the European Economic Community created serious social dislocation in a great many Inuit communities. The rate of suicide went up as did alcoholism and drug abuse. Mr. Gordon Wray, the Minister of Economic Development and Tourism in the Northwest Territories, recently indicated in an interview he gave to the Toronto Globe and Mail that:
Animal-right groups opposed the slaughter of harp-seal pups in Newfoundland and succeeded in mobilizing the European Community to boycott seal skins in 1984. In the NWT, where most sealing is done, the hunt took only adult seals. Residents insist the centuries-old practice maintained a delicate ecological balance, as well as holding together Inuit communities.
In 1980-81, sealers earned $884,000 but this dropped, after the EC ban, to only $77,000 in 1983-84, and then to a negligible $26,000 last year.
Mr. Wray said that the social dislocation inflicted on these communities is staggering. Children who were raised to revere sealing as an honourable livelihood saw television commercials portraying their parents as criminals. During the same period 21 of 29 Northwest Territories coastal communities received substantial increases in social assistance. Therefore, this European move created social chaos in the Inuit communities, took away the livelihood of these people, and placed them on social assistance taking away their self-respect and dignity.
In northern Ontario the Indian people who belong to the so-called Treaty Nine Area are organized as the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation. Many of these people depend on trapping as their only source of income. Recently there was an editorial in the Wawatay news, an aboriginal peoples' newspaper. That editorial said that trapping "means a way of life that retains a traditional economic activity".
Eighty-five to 90 per cent of the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation people are engaged in trapping to some extent. Many are only part-time trappers. In the western James Bay coastal communities 80 to 85 per cent of the people trap. The unemployment rate in these communities is between 80 and 85 per cent. These people trap in order to supplement their meagre incomes, to supplement their social assistance.
Trapping, hunting, and fishing are all part of living with the land, in harmony with the land, and off the land. Not to understand that is to lead one to a false and fallacious conclusion. It is that the furbearing animals of this country are systematically being destroyed because there is a fur industry and because people go out trapping. That is far, far from the truth.
I want to point out that animal-rights activists tend mainly to be urbanites and what they fail to realize in their misguided zeal is that it is the growth of cities, its building of superhighways and airports that have been far more detrimental to wildlife than trapping will ever be. It is the loss of habitat to overdevelopment and industrialization which is the real danger to wildlife, not trapping.
How ironic it is that we are today, in this House, I expect unanimously resisting and opposing a proposal that will go before the European Parliament, when in Europe we had those successive European wars in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with the slaughter of millions upon millions of young men. This paved the way for massive industrial expansion in Europe and pollution on a basis that was never known anywhere in the world before. Now these same European nations, at least speaking through some of their representatives in the European Parliament, want to restrict the importation of wild furs from Canada. It is more than ironic, it is crass hypocrisy. Trapping is not a threat to furbearing animals.
In fact, the Aboriginal Affairs Committee heard testimony that the furbearing population in Canada is at least as high if not higher than when Europeans first came to this continent. After 400 years of commercial fur trade, most furbearing species in North America are still flourishing, and those few species today that are in danger, are threatened mainly because their habitat has befen destroyed. I believe that animal rights activists are best advised to focus their attention on the humane treatment of pets and other domestic animals.
The trapping of wild animals in Canada involves the survival of a culture, a way of life. I am speaking of the culture and way of life of aboriginal people. If these city-dwelling zealots who, in my view, constitute a part of the urban lunatic fringe, have their way, they will be responsible for nothing other than cultural genocide. The proposal planned for the European Parliament will contribute to the destruction of that culture and that way of life.
July 20, 1988

Let me speak about some of the concerns of these people, which they have inflated beyond all reason. In Ontario there is a native education program. It is sponsored by the federal and provincial Governments. In the past year over 500 aboriginal trappers were exposed to more modern and humane methods of managing and harvesting furbearing animals. Educational programs such as these, plus the millions of dollars that are being spent on trap research, are in my mind the effective ways to combat the anti-trapping movement. The labelling of products, the boycotting of fur garments are illogical and silly ways of proceeding.
It should be noted in addition that for many trappers, the food value of the animals that are caught often surpasses the value of the fur pelt itself. In many remote areas there are often limited options for food. Most beaver, snowshoe hare, muskrat and bear whose skins are sold, are also used as food. We have studies that show that the value of the meat thus harvested is in many cases greater than the value of the fur itself.
The issue here is not one of abuse. Not at all. The issue here is not one of non-use. Not at all. The issue is one of wise use of a resource. In my experience, trappers are among the most active supporters of wildlife conservation. Why would they not be? Their own livelihood is involved. Of course they are conservationists. Fur trappers tend to be among the most conservationist-minded of people.
Recently, the Cochrane Area Fur Council wrote to me about their industry. In their letter they said: "Conservation means the wise use of natural resources".
I conclude by saying to the House that Europeans must be helped in their understanding and appreciation of aboriginal culture. Trapping is a vital aspect of that culture and by supporting this notice of motion today in the House we are saying to European countries, to the people of Europe: "Turn your attention to the relevant problems that exist on your own doorstep. Please do not reach out in an uninformed and selfrighteous manner and destroy an industry, a way of life and even a people which are indigenous to this nation of ours here in North America".
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity again today to address some remarks on the question of measures that have been proposed in other jurisdictions with regard to the labelling of fur. The measures that were first proposed in the British Parliament have, very happily, been withdrawn. But they are now within the European Parliament of the European Economic Community.
I believe those proposed regulations are profoundly misleading and profoundly dangerous to the basis on which international commerce and international relations are undertaken. They are profoundly misleading to the people who might read them.
Fur Industry
I am glad to join with my colleagues in all three Parties in extending thanks and recognition to the Government for the opportunity again to address this important question. As I recall, I was the second to the last speaker sometime after midnight on the morning of June 2nd when we were addressing the motion that had been put forward at that time. We heard from all three Parties, but I am glad to say that my Party participated most fully in that particular debate. I am pleased that all Parties and all Members who spoke were united in their concern for the impact these regulations might have on aboriginal people of this country.
Arriving very recently in Ottawa, I have not had the opportunity to research the exact procedure and stage of this proposed measure before the European Economic Community, but I think the specific stage is perhaps not so important as is the need and urgency for this House to get across to those major partners of Canada-and let them not forget it-in the European Economic Community that Canada does not appreciate this sort of interference and harassment of the longest standing, continuous commerce between our country and the European Economic Community.
I looked at the historical perspective in my speech of June 1 and 2, and I believe it is worth re-emphasizing. Let us remember that it was the European market that built up the fur industry in this country. Successive generations of European consumers, furriers, traders and merchants have dealt with successive generations of Canadian trappers, both aboriginal and non-aboriginal. This was done by means, of course, of the intermediaries the great trading companies and the co-operatives of today, such as the Ontario Trapping Association. Let us, above all, not forget that it was the fur trade that radically altered the economy, traditions and lifestyle of the aboriginal people, during what is considered to be a period of pre-history but about which more and more is becoming known. It led to some very drastic changes by the aboriginal people, by the Metis and by the early European trappers and traders in order to restructure the economy and life of North America at that time.
There was a time in this country when the fur trade was the largest part of the economy. There was a time when it was, so to speak, the fer de lance of exploration and economic development within Canada and the northern part of what is now the United States. Indeed, there was a time when the fur trade provided this country with its basic currency, its first universally accepted trading medium. That was the standard beaver, as it was known. The Hudson's Bay Company, and the Northwest company before it, kept their accounts not in pounds, shillings and pence, not in dollars and cents, but in what were called "made beaver", what we would now call a double-x large beaver pelt in prime, flattened and properly tanned. At one time it took a pile of made beaver as high as a musket to buy that same musket.

July 20, 1988
Fur Industry
Let us not forget that even as Canada grew and developed, and exploration pushed back the frontiers of the imported European civilization, in many parts of this country it was trapping and the fur trade that provided not only the basic raison d'etre of many communities but was the largest part of the economy in a whole region twice as large as the entire continent of Europe.
In examining this question today, we have to be very careful in our approach. We have to remember that mere oratory or rhetoric, and even, as important as it may be, the reiteration of the importance of fur trade to Canada's economy, particularly to the aboriginal people, is not the most effective thing we can do. What we have to do is to work towards an understanding of why these labelling regulations are being brought forward. We have to work towards a strategy to counteract the motives behind the introduction and proposals of such legislation or regulation.
I think it is worth spending some time to consider the psychology that underlies the attempts to have Canadian fur mislabelled, or, I would say, labelled in a misleading fashion that is designed to deter some consumers, although, frankly, I am surprised at the store that is set by this because I do not believe it would be terribly effective even if it went into effect.
As the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), a defender of aboriginal people in this House over two decades, pointed out, it is primarily because of the psychology of urbanization. Urbanization in the European continent even since the Second World War, which was largely fought on that continent, has taken the proportion of urban dwellers to near double pre-war levels, somewhere, 1 believe, in the region of 80 per cent. That has led to a divorce between the people and their sustenance. It has led to a divorce between the people of the European Economic Community and their environment, a divorce between them and those who supply them with the means of everyday living.
Along with that divorce from nature has grown an unreal psychological environment in which people are raised. I should know because, after all, I was raised in what is still the largest city in the European continent. The feelings that arise very naturally within the minds of human beings are all too easily transferred and transmogrified because of the environment in which they live. We learn, and certainly people in Europe learn, to have respect for those who are near and dear to us, but increasingly that respect is set against an appreciation of the wider environment. It is said that there are children within the inner City of London who, at the age of nine years, have never seen a cow, yet drink milk every day. That does not surprise me because it is a long haul from that city out to the country where one could actually see a cow.
In an age of increasing affluence, people have come to identify animals not with the milk in the glass, the slice of roast beef on the table, the leather on the shoes they wear, but with the hamsters and the gerbil, the pussy-cat and the lapdog, the pets they keep on an everyday basis and for which, understandably, they have feelings.
Another sad consequence of that divorce from the natural environment, even with television bringing the images to our homes on a daily and even hourly basis seems to be a divorce from an understanding of the plight of fellow humans. There are people starving on the sidewalks of Calcutta, there are the wasted fields of drought-scorched Ethiopia, the flood victims in Bangladesh and the victims of malnutrition and elevated child mortality rates in the Andes, among the aboriginal people of the southern American continent. It seems that as a society we are losing our understanding and compassion for our fellow human beings who live in those circumstances.
There has to be, of course, a specific spur to action, to mobilize the psychological factors I have described. We might very well ask, and would, I hope, ask our foreign Minister, who did such good work with his namesake, the junior trade Minister from Great Britain, Mr. Allan Clark, to ask these questions of the European Community. Why does the European community not take action against bullfighting? Why does it not take action against the obscene sport of fox-hunting which is still carried out in the United Kingdom? Why does it not take action against the barbarous practice of many French farmers who nail to the floor the feet of geese and force corn down their gullets in order to produce pate de foie grasl
Let us not be seen to be pointing fingers because we all are prey in some degree to such actions and such motivations. The fact is that the European Economic Community has decided to take action on fur trapping and fur products because it is much easier to try to beat up an external "enemy" than to address some of the grave divisions and dissensions within European society, whether it be on a single country or on a pan-European basis.
We should understand that motive. We should be very clear to the countries of the European Economic Community that we do understand those motives and that Canada is not without the ability to resort to trade sanctions and trade measures if indeed such regulations are passed within the European Parliament.
My hon. friends from Timiskaming and Cochrane- Superior have said it well already. The trapper is a conserver. The trapper is a harvester. There is no species on the North American continent that has been endangered by trapping. The passenger pigeon was exterminated because of the desire for food, not by trapping. The true enemy of the survival of wildlife species is indeed the destruction of habitat, the destruction that is carried out as a by-product of economic activity, it would appear, within the European Economic Community and, indeed, in many other jurisdictions because environmental protection regulations are not perfected here in Canada, not perfected in any jurisdiction.
July 20, 1988

Let us not forget the number of species that have been exterminated in Europe by habitat erosion. Let us point out to the Europeans that it is by protection of the habitat, of which having communities of people and having active trappers is an essential part, that species will be saved from extinction.
Turning briefly to the cruelty issue, nobody will pretend that it is in some way an amiable experience for the animal. But we have heard a great deal of dissimulation and misinformation from European sources, and even from so-called animal rights advocates in this country, as to the nature of what an animal does or does not feel, and particularly as to the nature of what animals are being trapped.
There is no large-scale problem with so-called unwanted or scrap species. Trappers came before our committee on the hearings that the Hon. Member for Timiskaming mentioned. They said: "Not once in my career as a trapper have I taken an animal other than the animal that I wanted to take in that trap". I believe that is a point which has to be made because, of course, the propaganda films show species that cannot be used by the trapper struggling in the trap. We have to emphasize just how rare that is.
I think that the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior also made the point very well as to the economic value of the nonfur part of the animal. I would say that it is no misrepresentation to say that all the trappers whom I have known respect the animals with which they deal. I say respect in terms of the aboriginal peoples' spirituality, the spirit of the animal that they are using, using because of their profound belief that the creator put the animals there for their use and that while the animals are used respectfully they will return. When they are abused, the animals go. This is something which runs through the legends of all the aboriginal peoples of Canada. That surely is the representation of the effects of successful conservation as practised by aboriginal trappers in the country since time immemorial.
Because of the shortage of time I must turn to the question of what will happen. The seal ban showed us what will happen. It showed us that the eradication of an economic base and the consequent deterioration of the social fabric of communities that depended upon that seal hunt constituted as an end nothing more than a cultural genocide of the people who were victimized, the people in the Arctic who were victimized by the eradication of that hunt. The people of Nishnawbe-Aski and the people of the Grand Council Treaty Three reserves whom I represent know that this could be the final straw, the final, destructive, demoralizing, alienating straw that would tell them that the people who came to their land, emissaries in a commercial sense of the European Market, have now seen them as having outlived their usefulness, and are preparing to discard them and to turn their communities into little more than welfare ghettos.
That is a consequence which I will always be determined to fight. I hope that all Members of the House will be determined to join me in that particular fight.
Fur Industry
The fragile economic base of these communities, the terrifying pace of change that they have seen will be doubled and redoubled if this sort of measure ever takes effect. In a community of my experience, Weagama Lake, it went from one plane a week to five planes a day in three years. They went from paths to roads in a similar period of time. The blows, the psychological impacts, the sense of being hemmed in that the people of Nishnawabe-Aski, the Cree, the Ojibway of the communities of Grand Council Treaty Three have had to endure will be doubled and redoubled if this sort of measure ever takes effect.
In summation, we must examine what we can do-because it is of only limited usefulness to fulminate-to spread the information. It is only of limited usefulness even to undertake educational campaigns within the European Economic Community. We have to come down to the hard pragmatic measures that will have some effect in blunting this initiative.
To do so we have to call upon the support of our largest trading partner, the United States. After all, the United States does export more fur than does Canada. While the fur industry is of lesser significance proportionately in the United States, as a whole it is indeed larger than the Canadian fur industry, which must come as a surprise to some.
Above all, we must try to take away the main ammunition and the main thrust which is being used by these animal rights advocates which is, of course, cruelty. I believe we can do that by continuing the excellent programs of trap replacement that have been started, and the very well supported, particularly by the trappers themselves, trapper education programs. We must reach out to the people who are proposing these regulations. We must expand and intensify our research in humane trapping methods. We must spend some money and make some effort to ensure that those who have the opportunity to decide on these matters are brought to Canada and shown the economic, the social, the cultural context, and also the techniques of humane trapping as it is fast developing in Canada today.
If we can take those measures, then I believe we do have some chance of blunting this initiative which, if it is successful, could have some very sad consequences and some very tragic consequences in the aboriginal communities of this country for whom the fur industry is still the economic mainstay.
Hear, hear!

Income Tax Act and Related Acts INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
July 20, 1988

The House resumed, from Tuesday, July 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and the Federal PostSecondary Education and Health Contribution Act, 1977, and certain related Acts, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs; and the amendment of Mr. Garneau (p. 17724), and the subamendment of Mr. Boudria (p. 17770).

Mr. Speaker, during the debate on Bill C-139 many of my colleagues discussed how tax reform benefits individual taxpayers, but comparatively little attention has been devoted to another vital area of reform, corporate tax reform. Canada needs a reformed corporate tax system that is competitive internationally, more efficient and market-oriented, and fairer.
In the past, Canada's corporate tax system suffered from serious problems. Its capacity to raise revenues was seriously eroded over the years by a multitude of special tax deductions and other incentives. While each special preference was introduced to address a particular problem, the number of these breaks has enabled many profitable corporations to reduce their tax liability or pay no tax at all.
As a member of the Finance Committee I recall that the life insurance industry in particular paid little or no tax for the last 10 years. At one point in the hearings a chairman of the board of one of the largest companies, when questioned on whether or not the company paid tax, stated that it did not. When corrected by a vice-president he admitted that the company had received oil royalties and had paid a bit of tax on those. However, there are some sectors where the tax system has become totally unfair.
One of the problems is that the sheer number of incentives distorted market signals and led to inefficient uses of Canada's resources. It got to the point where tax considerations directed investments instead of sound business considerations. Again, if I could direct my thoughts back a few years to my former company where, from time to time, I worked on acquisitions, it was amazing how often the number one consideration when looking at a possible acquisition would be the tax situation. We did look at the type of services and the market share, but time and again the number one consideration would be the tax situation.
Our corporate tax system must remain competitive in an increasingly competitive world economy. Many of our trading partners have overhauled their tax systems to reduce tax rates and improve efficiency. Canada's general corporate tax rate was much higher than that of the United States and the United Kingdom. If we fail to narrow this gap, firms can arrange their operations to pay their taxes at lower rates to other countries rather than to Canada.
From time to time our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) may have been criticized for moving ahead with this. I can
recall perhaps two years ago asking the Minister of Finance if he was going to move ahead with comprehensive tax reform. At that time his answer was that we were moving in that direction as a Government, but did not plan a comprehensive tax reform. But the world and realities change, and when the United States, in particular, moved ahead with its comprehensive tax reform, the Minister of Finance was wise to change his mind on that factor for the reasons that we have already touched upon.
Our proposals for reform of the corporate tax system will resolve these problems and achieve the three major goals we set out in the White Paper. First, profitable corporations will pay a larger share of the total tax burden. Corporate income tax will be a more predictable and reliable source of revenue.
Second, many special tax breaks will be eliminated or reduced. This will pay for the lower personal and corporate tax rates. It will return the profit motive to investment by rewarding success. It will encourage investment decisions based more on economic factors than on tax considerations. Certainly, some proposals of the previous Government went completely off the rails. I think particularly of the scientific research tax credit. When that was announced by the former Government it was believed that it would cost taxpayers something in the order of $200 million. We all know that that was poorly thought out, ill-conceived, and inadequately controlled to the point that the best estimate now is that this initiative will cost the taxpayers of Canada in excess of $3 billion. Some serious mistakes have been made. However, the Minister of Finance proceeds cautiously and carefully and he is making tremendous headway.
Third, corporate tax rates will be reduced. This will promote growth and job creation by maintaining a corporate tax system that is competitive with other countries.
There has been general support for the goals and the outlines of these proposals. We consulted extensively with the corporate sector and the public, and listened carefully to what they said. We considered all proposed modifications in the light of the goals of our reform, and as they would affect other elements of tax reform. We made some changes to improve the original proposals.
The rates of corporate tax are the same as those set out in the White Paper. Effective July 1, the general federal rate dropped to 28 per cent from 36 per cent. The small business rate fell from 15 per cent to 12 per cent. The rate for manufacturing will be phased down to 23 per cent by 1991.
The White Paper's proposals for broadening the corporate tax base will generally be implemented. While there will be fewer special tax preferences, not all tax incentives will be removed. The tax system will continue to recognize the importance of incentives for investment in resources, manufacturing, R and D, and small businesses, among others. The incentives that remain will be fairer and more effective in supporting economic growth and regional development.
July 20, 1988

For example, we improved our proposals on flow-through shares to ensure they remain an attractive investment vehicle and a benefit for junior resource companies; the proposed limitation on claimable investment tax credits has been increased to ensure that our tax regime for R and D remains among the most attractive in the world; and our proposal for capitalization of interest on vacant land will be modified so it does not affect small home building firms.
Concerns about the fairness of the system were aroused because of the number of profitable firms not paying tax. Our proposals, when fully implemented, will mean a substantial decline in the number of such companies. Tax reform will reduce by one-half the number of profitable corporations that pay no tax. Those that remain will either be firms in cyclical industries that have experienced significant economic losses in prior years, or will be firms in industries which receive incentives directed at important national priorities. These priorities include promoting regional development, ensuring a healthy and active resource sector, and encouraging research and development that will provide jobs for Canadians in the future.
A combination of a broader base and lower rates will produce more revenue, bringing the over-all tax system into better balance. Corporate tax revenues as a share of general tax revenues will increase from 15.6 per cent in 1987-88 to 17.2 per cent in 1991-92. In dollar terms, the federal corporate tax revenues will increase by about $5.5 billion over the next five years. That is approximately 10 per cent higher. Across the entire economy, corporate tax reform will strengthen the incentive for firms to invest in profitable ventures. The rate of tax on the return from new investment will be reduced. The tax treatment of capital will continue to encourage risk-taking initiative, growth and job creation. There will be less variation of tax paid by different sectors. Sectors which formerly paid below average taxes, such as finance and life insurance, will pay higher effective tax rates. Sectors that paid higher than average taxes, such as trade, services and construction, will pay lower effective tax rates. At the same time, the tax rate for small business will continue to provide a major incentive for entrepreneurs to create jobs and to promote economic growth.
The federal small business tax rate of 12 per cent is less than one-half of the tax imposed on large businesses. In addition, owners of shares in small businesses will also benefit from the full $500,000 exemption in capital gains on these shares, to reward success in private entrepreneurship.
Corporate tax reform is a key element of the Government's over-all plan to position the Canadian economy and to take
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
advantage of the opportunities in the 1990s. I urge all Members of this House who want to see a stronger Canadian economy to vote with me in favour of Bill C-139.
Just before closing, if I might touch on a couple of other points, let me say that it is vitally important that we get on with this legislation. Those people involved in tax planning and running business know that one of the big problems on something like this is delays and uncertainty. We must get on with this so that people can plan confidently and not be wondering continually when this legislation might be passed.
I think that the confidence of our Finance Minister, as I mentioned earlier, grows by the day and by the month. We have here a Finance Minister who in the past three years has made projections of what the deficit would be. Every single year of the last three has come in on or under the projections. This latest one will be something like $1 billion lower than forecast. A lot of Canadians would not realize this, but that is the best three-year record in 45 years.
I think we have tremendous confidence in this Minister. Let us get behind him, let us get this legislation passed, and let us get on with the increases that will occur in the corporate sector, to help provide lower taxes for the consumers.
We know that four out of five consumers will be paying less tax, and nine out of 10 seniors will be paying less tax. This is a great over-all package. People will nit-pick on certain aspects of it, but on balance it is a super package, one that a lot of Canadians will benefit from, and I think we are moving in a very excellent way to a fairer system.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member would be willing at least to acknowledge that what appears to be tax reductions that are contained in the Bill before us really do not, when looked at over the picture of tax increases of low and middle-income Canadians over the last four years, give back to low-income Canadians the amounts that this Government has taken away from them in the whole four-year picture.

Mr. Speaker, of all Parties to start trying to slow down this Bill, that should be the last Party. It is the Party that put us into a deficit situation year after year, so much so that now the entire deficit of $29 billion to $30 billion is devoted not to reducing the debt but devoted 100 per cent to paying the interest on that debt.
Now, let us have our focus on moving ahead. I have described the package in the corporate sector, certainly. There is a lot being done. We must get on with the business and eliminate the uncertainty that exists out there. I will quote the following from The Globe and Mail issue of April 25th:

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
If an election were called before stage one became law, tax reform would die
and the current system would stand until new legislation was introduced.
That would create chaos. "I hope Brian Mulroney isn't irresponsible enough
to call an election before the bill gets through the House."
The person who made that comment was the Liberal finance critic, Raymond Garneau.

Mr. Speaker, I think it must be obvious to everyone in this Chamber, including the large crowd in the gallery, that the Hon. Member made no reference at all to my question in the statement that he just made, or any attempt to answer it or to explain away, which I thought he might do, the point that I tried to make. I called on the Hon. Member and asked him to recognize that the reductions that are contained in Bill C-130, for most Canadians, lower and middle-income Canadians in particular, do not restore the tremendous tax increases that those very groups have sustained since this Government took office four years ago.
I know that there was a deficit to deal with and that it is a legitimate option to increase taxes. I am calling on the Member to recognize that the taxes that have been increased are not the taxes that are on the richest in society, on the highest income earners. The taxes that have been increased are on the lowest earners and middle-income Canadians.
I call on the Hon. Member to admit that this is the case, at least out of a sense of honesty.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are going to get a chance to judge fairly quickly what this Government has done.
Hear, hear!
It has been a great package in total.
They cannot wait.

They are going to see that four out of five Canadians are going to be paying less tax, and nine out of 10 seniors will pay less tax. Some sectors are finally going to be paying their share. I mentioned that some people might try to slow down this package in certain isolated areas, but in total I can only stress again-and you mentioned people watching this in the gallery and elsewhere-I know that they will be, but I know that they are also examining our record as a Government, the record of the Finance Minister, which I will just highlight again.
It is the first time in 45 years that we have had three successive projections of being on or below the forecast. That is a responsible performance compared to the totally irresponsible performance of the Liberal Government. I can remember the Liberal Government adjusting its projections on deficits by the week, not too many years ago. I think it is pretty clear in which Party, in which Government the people of Canada are going to have their confidence. They are not going to return it back to the irresponsible bunch that they had for about 16 years.
Hear, hear!
Time for a change.

Mr. Speaker, I will say a few words to the Hon. Member who sits from time to time on the Finance Committee and who does his work there. In a sense I think that there is something wrong with the Conservative tax reform. It seems to suit the residents of the Hon. Member's constituency perhaps more than the average Canadian. Is it fair to have a so-called tax reform which winds up leaving only one group among Canadians paying less tax on their income than they paid in 1984, namely people who are earning more than a $100,000 a year? Is it fair to have a tax system which will leave the corporate share of tax revenues to the Government of Canada, to drop it down to 17 per cent in 1991, which in fact is lower than the 20 per cent share that corporations paid of tax revenues in 1984? When the Conservatives came to power, corporations were paying a larger share of federal revenues than they will be paying in 1991, after this particular and so-called tax reform is mature.
Perhaps the Hon. Member could say whether it is fair to have tax reform which will give tax cuts of only $140 to poor people earning under $15,000 a year but which, according to the Government's own figures, will give a tax cut of some $4,165 on average to three out of four families earning over $100,000. Is that fair? Is that just? Could the Hon. Member take those facts into a pub in Kamloops or Newfoundland and defend that? Could he take that to a group of families and justify the unfairness of a system where the tax credit which people get if they have children is the magnificent sum of only $65 a year? Is that fair? Could the Hon. Member say, if he agrees with me that these things are not fair, why the Government is going ahead with a tax reform which essentially is unfair to families, unfair to average Canadians, and fair only to the rich and to corporations?

Mr. Speaker, the system we are recommending, the package, I say is fair. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) has been on the Finance Committee. I have been on it for almost four years now. We have had a tremendous amount of consultation and have done a lot of research. Our committee visited Washington. Every aspect of this package has been thoroughly looked at and analysed.
Let me highlight again some of the benefits and who will be paying less. Income taxes will be reduced for 9.7 million households, over 85 per cent of all households, by an average of $490. About 850,000 lower-income Canadians will have their income tax reduced to zero or will receive refundable credits. In other words, they will be coming right off the tax rolls. Income taxes will be cut for about 1.3 million of the 1.4 million households which have at least one person in them aged 65 and over. About 250,000 elderly Canadians will have their income tax reduced to zero. Personal income tax will be lower for all ranges of income. Most taxpayers whose income
July 20, 1988

consists primarily of salary or wages, family allowance or standard pension and retirement revenue will receive tax reductions. Last, net personal income tax revenue to the federal Government will be reduced by about $12 billion, not $12 million but $12 billion coming off the personal side. I say that that is a giant leap in fairness.

Mr. Speaker, I have to say that it is a giant leap backwards. When I talk to my constituents and to average Canadians and ask them what they think about this tax thing, whether they think this tax reform is a good idea, the reaction I get is: "You know, I am not sure what it is, but I am not seeing as much money at home as I was four years ago. I am not sure where it is going, but I know it is going".
This is a product of two things, Mr. Speaker. On the one hand, real incomes of Canadians have not been rising. On the other hand, the bite of the tax collector has been increasing on those average Canadians. As we calculate it, it is an average of $ 1,500 or so in tax increases on the average Canadian with an income of perhaps $30,000 or $35,000 a year since 1984, and tax reform will give about $300 or $350 back. If you have to give up $4 and you get $1, you are not better off; you are worse off. It seems to me that that is the situation which prevails with tax reform. The Government will say: "Look at last year and look at what is happening this year". The Government will ignore the consistent pattern of tax increases on average Canadians imposed by the Conservatives at the same time as they cut taxes on wealthy Canadians by the capital gains exemption and stuff like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: And the farmers.

I would correct the Hon. Member's recollection as well. In committee when my colleague from Regina West and I raised the question about the rates and asked "why are we giving such cuts to people who are wealthy and doing so little for people on average incomes", the chairman simply said: "We are not discussing that here", and we went on to something else. My colleague and I had two choices. We could have either co-operated on the areas where the Finance Committee was able to co-operate productively, or we could have simply walked out and said: "This is a Tory show". We were constructive and chose to participate. I think the committee made some constructive suggestions, but in this area we were completely excluded from the game.
I am really surprised at my hon. friend from Don Valley suggesting that this was looked at. It was not looked at all. It was on the Tory agenda that the Conservatives wanted to give very large tax cuts to wealthy Canadians, a sharp reduction in taxes for many corporations, and to do that with a small cut for average Canadians, which is far less than the increases in tax they have had since 1984.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words concerning this very extensive Bill. I have listened to Hon. Members argue about who is responsible for this tax increase or who is responsible for that tax increase. I
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
have heard them argue that there was not a tax increase, there is not going to be a tax increase, there is going to be a tax decrease, or there is not going to be a tax decrease. For those of us who help people in our constituencies fill out their income tax returns, one thing is obvious. People are paying more income tax as the years go by than they did in previous years.
If you took the last four years and filled out the income tax returns for the same person, you would discover that the individual is paying more income tax as each year goes by. I do not know where Hon. Members are getting all these facts and figures about people paying less income tax. All I can see is that they are paying more income tax.
I suppose there are only two groups of people. I was thinking about this as I was glancing at some portions of the Bill a few moments ago. One group are millionaires. Of course I do not fill out income tax returns for millionaires; I do not know any. In the place from where I come on the northeast coast of Newfoundland we do not have any millionaires sitting around doing their income tax. They would not fill them out anyway. They would have a chartered accountant do it.
I want to make an honest to goodness logical suggestion for the Government of Canada on this one point about income tax.
I have here in my hand a list of some 200 communities in Alberta, about 600 communities in British Columbia, about 400 communities in Newfoundland, and so on. This year these communities qualify for a new tax break. Granted, some of the communities are pretty small. If you live in these communities you will probably gain, if you pay taxes, about $2,000 to $2,500 on your income tax return when you fill it out. I noticed that some of the communities do not have anybody living in them. There is a community in Newfoundland called Exploits. Only two people live in Exploits. They are Richard Wells and Lydia. They have lived there all their lives. Richard is a pensioner. Also, some of the communities are quite large. If you examine the list here, you will find that there are perhaps 50 communities in my federal riding.
The Minister stood in this House the other day and spoke about fairness in taxation. He spoke about the fact that the Government of Canada has brought fairness into the tax system. It is a funny thing, but I noticed that some communities which have now been listed for northern benefits are on the border of Canada and the United States. Some communities listed for northern benefits are in southern Newfoundland, but there are none listed in northern Newfoundland. This tells me that there is something drastically wrong with the regulations the Government has brought in.
Granted, this is a very difficult situation. You know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker, because you know about that northern section of Quebec and the Gaspe coast where a great many of these communities are located. It is very difficult to come up with criteria for the tax law as it relates to deductions

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
being administered fairly. In other words, how do we define an isolated community?
We do not define an isolated community the way the Government of Canada did a few days ago, that is, by saying that everything above the 55th parallel is isolated and everything below the 55th parallel is not isolated. It does not make much sense to have the entire Burin Peninsula and the entire south coast of Newfoundland getting benefits while the islands up North do not get them.
The Government of Canada, though it has appointed a commission of inquiry to look into the matter, could have come up with a more sensible way of distributing these benefits than jt has. It has sent to each person living in those communities a special form to fill out to see if he or she qualifies. Looking at the communities and areas that qualify, one would have to say that the person who made up that list really used no common sense whatsoever in determining what was isolated and what was not. The commission of inquiry, as I understand it, is starting its hearings in Newfoundland next week.
There is another clause in the Bill that I want to comment on. That is the clause that deals with the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Minister, in his wisdom, has brought in an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act here dealing with amounts of money owed by the employer to the Receiver General for Canada, the Government of Canada. The Government is now imposing a penalty on the employer. The penalty is as follows: the employer shall pay to the Receiver General that amount computed from the day on which it was owed to the day of the remittance of the amount to the Receiver General for Canada, and the normal interest rate shall be charged.
If the Government is going to amend that Section of the Unemployment Insurance Act, surely to goodness it should have then revised the penalties that apply to the recipients of unemployment insurance benefits when that same Section is in violation. Let me tell Hon. Members what that is under this particular Section of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The recipient of unemployment insurance would have to have his unemployment insurance reduced over a period of time to satisfy the debt owed the Crown. The employer, in the case of uninsurability, gets no penalty whatsoever except that he gets back the money that he paid in.
The Government of Canada, in changing the law as it relates to Subsection 68(6) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, certainly should have addressed the problem in relation to the recipients of unemployment insurance as well as the employers. As I say, the principle of fairness in the Unemployment Insurance Act goes out the window when one examines the Northern Benefits and Isolated Posts Act. It goes out the window because I do believe that politics came into play very recently when some Members in this Chamber got a hold of two Ministers and had whole areas designated as being eligible for these particular allowances.
The Bill itself also amends the Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977, and the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act. I do hope that more Hon. Members will address these very important subjects as the day goes on.

Mr. Speaker, I am just curious. I know that the Hon. Member has been here before, and I know that the Liberal Party has been critical of the Government because of a tax reform which favours too much the rich and wealthy corporations.
I seem to recall that back in 1981, when Senator Mac-Eachen was the Minister of Finance, the Liberal Party came in with a Budget which was ostensibly meant to broaden the base and at the same time lower the tax rates for wealthy Canadians by a substantial amount. I seem to recall as well that after a good deal of pressure from the business community and other friends of the Liberal Party, the loophole plugging exercise, the broadening of the base that was meant to take place, was in fact reversed. At the same time, the Liberal Party did not put back up to previous levels the reductions of taxes for wealthy Canadians.
I also recall that when the Liberals were in power, beginning with the present Leader of the Liberal Party, in fact, there was a series of measures which had the effect of reducing the tax burden on corporations through accelerated depreciation and various other types of allowances which, among other things, led to an enormous piling up of deferred taxation on the part of the corporate sector, to an erosion of corporate tax revenues and to many of the injustices in corporate taxation which average Canadians have been so concerned about.
My hon. friend comes from a part of the country where that kind of thing really is not very tolerable because there are not many wealthy Canadians in his constituency. How is it that he was able at that time to let pass without comment the fact that the Liberals were reducing taxes on the wealthy just as the Tories are reducing taxes on the wealthy today, and that the Liberals were reducing taxes on corporations, just as the Tories are reducing taxes on corporations today? Perhaps the Hon. Member can tell us if there was any difference between the Liberal Party at that time and the Conservative Party today, because I cannot see very much difference.

Mr. Speaker, I can remember when the NDP- no, I cannot remember when the NDP formed the Government of Canada. It is very difficult to follow the hon. gentleman's logic. For the past four years, the hon. gentleman has been blaming the Conservative Government for drastically raising taxes on everyone, and he has been saying that prior to that the Liberals were drastically increasing taxes on everyone. The Hon. Member knows full well, however, that as far as federal income taxes are concerned, income taxes for ordinary Canadians took a fairly substantial drop in years prior. When I say "substantial", I mean that when a person filled out his income tax form at least he got a little more. I am talking
July 20, 1988

about the average Canadian, and by "average" I mean average in my riding.
What is average in my riding? Average in my riding is $8,000 or $9,000 a year. The Hon. Member does not know very many people who make $8,000 or $9,000 a year, I am sure. He does not represent fishermen. He does not represent the primary producers of Canada. He knows a lot about the corporate sector and what taxes it is paying.
I do not know anything about the corporate sector. All I know about is ordinary, producing Canadians. When the Liberal Government was in power, ordinary Canadians were the primary concern. I have seen incredible changes take place in the past four years since the Conservatives have been in government. Most of them have been to the detriment of these primary producers, these average Canadians who pay through the nose, day in and day out.
These average Canadians do not know, and I am afraid that I must claim some ignorance here and say that I do not know, what is the corporate tax structure. I have not got a clue. I do not know what happened under the Trudeau regime with corporate taxes. All I know is that ordinary Canadians benefited greatly under the Liberal administrations year after year. All I have seen in the last four years has been programs disappearing. All the assistance programs have disappeared. Look at all the insurance programs for fishermen; they were thrown out the window. All the assistance programs for boat building were thrown out the window. Why? Perhaps it was because they went against the wishes of the United States of America.
However, I can assure the Hon. Member of the NDP, the people who back in the mid-1970s supported the International Fund for Animal Welfare to get rid of the seal hunt, that under the Liberal Government the ordinary Canadians, the producers of Canada, are always looked out for first and foremost, not like under this present regime.
Oh, George, I don't believe you said that.

Mr. Speaker, while I have great respect for the Hon. Member, and while I know he speaks out for his constituents, there is a kind of blindness on the part of members of the Liberal Party, particularly when they are in government.
I have done a bit of research on this question. It does not affect Newfoundland directly, but it affects people with very modest incomes living in the east end of Montreal. I wanted to find out what was happening and who was speaking on their behalf between 1980 and 1984 when the Liberals were in power. I took the trouble to look at the legislative and parliamentary record of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) who is well known here as a voice of the people, at least oyer the last two or three years. During the time that Montreal's economy was going down the drain, when
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
