basic industries were shutting down almost every day, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie did not say a word. This man, who was such a defender of the rights of pensioners when the Conservative Government tried to deindex pensions in 1985, actually spoke up for deindexing public service pensions when the Liberal Party brought in the six and five program two or three years earlier. Yet there was not a peep, not a word was heard from him about Montreal.
It seems to me the problem with Liberal Members coming from poorer parts of Canada is that they walked on the other side of the street. They turned a blind eye when the Minister of Finance of the day cut tax rates on wealthy Canadians from over 60 per cent to the levels that prevailed before the Conservatives came to power. They turned a blind eye when the Government brought in accelerated depreciation schedules and other tax devices which made the whole tax fraternity and the corporate sector jump with joy.
The Hon. Member says he does not know anything about corporate taxes or accelerated depreciation. He had a responsibility to know about those things because during the time the Liberals were in power they were bleeding Canadians dry by putting so many tax breaks in the hands of wealthy Canadians and corporations. They did not take all the benefits away from average Canadians. What they did instead was run up the deficit in order to give those privileges to wealthy Canadians. That is a policy which tries to benefit everyone at the same time, but it led the country close to bankruptcy.
That is why I ask the Hon. Member why he and his colleagues were not vigorously on their feet to condemn the Government of the day in 1980 when its major priority for taxation seemed to be to cut taxes on the wealthy, just like the Conservatives today.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that accelerated depreciation is certainly not a major subject of importance in my riding. It certainly was not an election issue. Accelerated depreciation?
That sounds like growing old fast.

Yes. That is certainly not a subject of any great importance in my riding. However, I would certainly welcome the NDP running a campaign on it in Newfoundland. I would certainly welcome that kind of competition. Accelerated depreciation!
The Hon. Member is probably correct in one thing. That is, you will always be able to look back on what the Conservatives did and what the Liberals did, but you will never be able to look back on what the NDP did.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Burnaby.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The people don't want the NDP.

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts

Mr. Speaker, the people will certainly be making a clear decision in the next election, and it is about time that we had a real change from the worn out and discredited policies of the Liberals of the past and those policies of the Conservatives of today. The people of Canada are going to vote for New Democrats and a Government led by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). That is what is going to happen in the next election, and we are looking forward to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You are a bunch of bluffers.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on what the Government calls tax reform but which is in fact nothing of the sort. Instead of reforming the tax system in a meaningful way, it shifts the burden to the poor and powerless from the wealthy and the corporate elite. That is the effect of Tory tax reform.
I want to make it very clear that in the next federal election, and we say the time for that is now, the people should have a right to speak out on the record of the Government and voice their concerns about the proposed trade deal. A central theme for New Democrats in that election will be the question of fairness. What area of government policy is more lacking in fairness than the tax system?
What we are seeing with Tory tax reform is a move by the Government away from a progressive tax system, to a system in which, rather than taxing people on income, it is going to be taxing people on consumption. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) says that is all right because people choose whether or not they want to buy goods or services. What kind of unreal attitude is that? Tell a poor family, a single parent family, that they can choose whether or not to buy shoes and clothes for their children, that they can choose whether or not to spend money on housing, that they can choose whether or not to buy essentials to provide for their family. Of course that is nonsense. By moving from taxation of income to taxation of consumption the Government is moving away from progressive principles in the tax system.
As New Democrats we have clearly identified a number of important areas in which the Government should be tightening loopholes and increasing the progressive nature of the system. I want to pay tribute to my colleague from Ottawa Centre and my colleague from Regina East who have done such an outstanding job in committee and across this country in drawing to the attention of Canadians the unfairness and inequities in our tax system. In the four years of Conservative rule the share of taxes paid by the corporate sector has gone down from approximately 20 per cent in 1984 to some 15 per cent this year. Who is paying more in taxes? Of course, it is low and middle-income earners. That is the nature of Tory tax reform.
The Minister of Finance boasts that 850,000 Canadians are going to be removed from the tax rolls. He neglects to mention
that under four years of Tory rule over one million Canadians were added to the tax rolls. This kind of cynical shell game is obviously not going to wash with Canadians.
I have received extensive correspondence from my constituents in Burnaby on the unfairness of the Government's proposed tax reform. I want to share a couple of those letters with members of the House and those who are watching these proceedings across the country.
I received a letter, for example, from an 85-year-old constituent, Mr. Eric Button in North Burnaby. He wrote to me as follows:
Dear Svend:
Thank you for your latest Ottawa update. I enjoyed reading it.
In the last paragraph on income tax you did not mention the great change in the 1986 schedule over that of 1985. It seems to me that a multitude of poor people will be paying income tax this year. This will be the first time in 20 years that I have paid a tax ... We have always lived during our retirement time below the Government's poverty level.
He asked for an explanation. Why is it that for the first time in 20 years this elderly gentleman and his wife, who are struggling to survive on an income which is below the poverty line, are paying tax? He included copies of the schedules from the 1985 and 1986 tax tables. I examined them and, sure enough, under the Conservative Government taxes have in fact gone up substantially for the poorest in our society, including senior citizens.
I suppose we should not be surprised at that. After all, it was this same Government that attempted to deindex the pensions of senior citizens. It was only the angry outcry of seniors from right across this land that forced the Government to back down.
It is not surprising that a very respected national Seniors organization, the one voice: Canadian Seniors Network, in their response to the Government's White Paper on tax reform was severely critical of the proposals of the Government. They note that the fundamental principles of fairness, accountability, and stability are ignored when it comes to the proposals of the Government in the area of tax reform. We, as New Democrats, do not accept that.
We say that there is something very wrong with a tax system in which, in 1985, for example, 8,000 Canadians who made more than $50,000 paid not one penny in income tax. We say there is something wrong with that system. We say there is something wrong with a system in which, in 1984, over 1,400 people who had incomes in excess of $100,000 per year did not pay a penny in income tax.
We as New Democrats believe that the income tax system should be an important mechanism for the redistribution of income. We do not accept the philosophy of the Fraser Institute, for example, which suggests that we move to a flat rate system of taxation.
July 20, 1988

Under four years of Conservative Government we have seen an erosion of the fundamental principles of progressive income taxation and a very clear shift from income taxation to taxation on consumption. That shift is profoundly regressive and clearly attacks the poor in Canadian society.
The tax system should be used to redistribute income and wealth in our society. There is something fundamentally immoral about a society which is prepared to accept the fact that over one million of our children are poor while saying that some 8,000 individuals who make in excess of $50,000 a year have to pay no income tax whatsoever. There is something immoral about an economic system which condemns 700 children in the City of Vancouver and the municipality of Burnaby, which I have the honour to represent, to go to school hungry while the Government refuses to bring forward changes in the tax system which would ensure that such poverty is eliminated.
The same Government that refuses to tackle tax reform is prepared to spend in excess of $8 billion for nuclear submarines. What kind of madness is it that a Government is prepared to waste this kind of money? In fact, as my colleague from Winnipeg-Birds Hill points out, it is well in excess of $8 billion. In 1986 an estimated 102,000 Canadians were homeless. We want to spend $8 billion on nuclear submarines while people are homeless and hungry? As New Democrats we profoundly reject that.
What exactly does Tory tax reform mean and who does it benefit? Let us look at the figures. The most significant change under the tax proposals of the Minister of Finance is the reduction in the top tax rate on the highest income earners. In fact, the highest tax rate will drop from 34 per cent on incomes above $63,000 to 29 per cent on taxable incomes exceeding $55,000.
At the same time as the top tax rate is dropping the bottom rate is increasing. We are left with a situation, when provincial income tax is added in, in which the current top rate of 51 per cent is going to drop to 44 per cent but the bottom rate is going to increase from 9 per cent to 25 per cent. That is Tory tax reform-lower the marginal rates at the top and increase the marginal rates at the bottom. There is no sense of fairness or justice whatsoever.
It is interesting as well to consider the timing of these tax proposals. The tax reductions, of course, took effect on July 1 of this year. That meant a slight increase in the take-home pay of some employees. It is not entirely coincidental that this should be taking place on the eve of a federal election.
While there may be a slight decrease in taxes and a slight increase in take-home pay, the reality is that since 1984 a series of Conservative tax measures have increased sales and excise taxes substantially. The Government has taken literally hundreds of dollars out of the pockets of Canadians that it is now saying it is going to put back in the form of income tax reduction. We do not accept this. We do not accept so-called tax reform in which, as an example, a stockbroker who earns more than $200,000 a year is going to save $15,000 in tax while the Government continues to tax people who live below
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
the poverty line. That kind of so-called tax reform is completely unfair.
We say as well that it is time the Government took a serious look at tax expenditures in Canada. We have called for an annual review, an accountability of these tax expenditures which add up to in excess of $30 billion. Imagine what we could do with that money for social programs, post-secondary education, housing, and the environment. However, the Government refuses to consider that.
We have said that it is time that this country looks seriously at the taxation of capital gains. Why is it that 50 per cent of capital gains are exempt from taxes? The Government is now saying that it will move to tax 75 per cent of capital gains, but why do we not recognize that capital gains should be taxed just as any other income is taxed?
As long ago as 1967 Carter said it well "a buck is a buck is a buck". For that reason we, as New Democrats, have said that capital gains, aside from small businesses and the family farm, should be taxed fairly, just as is the income of those who work on an hourly and monthly basis. Why should those who earn their income from speculation in land, for example, be taxed at a lower rate than those who are employed? For that reason we have called upon the Government to recognize that it should be taxing capital gains as other income is taxed with the exception, as I said, of small businesses and family farms.
According to the proposed tax reform, the share of corporate taxation has gone down. Let us consider some of the rationale for this proposal. Why has the Government refused to tackle this question of capital gains? In 1984, the 1 per cent of taxpayers with incomes in excess of $100,000 received 30 per cent of all capital gains. Why are they not taxed fairly? That would reduce the burden on low and middle-income earners. Yet the Government is not prepared to take that step even though the Reagan Government in the United States has moved to tax capital gains at full rates, just like ordinary income.
The Government huffed and puffed about corporate taxation and suggested that it would make significant moves to increase the level of corporate taxation. However, it has done nothing of the sort. Since it took office in 1984, corporate taxes have increased 8 per cent, income taxes have gone up by approximately 45 per cent, and sales taxes have increased in excess of 67 per cent. That shows where the Government's heart really is. It is looking after its friends in the corporate elite and continuing to hit hard on low and middle-income earners.
What are the rationales for this so-called tax reform? Why has the Government not taken serious action? The Government says that by reducing the number of tax rates from 10 to 3 it will reduce the complexity of the system. What nonsense. The number of steps in the tax schedule has no bearing whatsoever on simplification.

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
It goes without saying that New Democrats have called for a more easily understandable tax system. The reality is that by reducing the top level of taxation from 34 per cent to 29 per cent, the Government is simply reducing the amount it will be collecting from the wealthiest in our society. Why should a secretary at Bell Canada who earns $28,000 pay a marginal tax rate that is only 5 percentage points below the rate paid by the chairperson of Bell Canada, Jean de Grandpre, whose salary last year was $977,300. Is that fairness? Is that a fair, equitable and just tax system? Of course not.
We believe that instead of lowering the marginal rate for the wealthiest and most affluent in our society, that rate should be increased to enable us to pay for the social programs that we value in this country.
That brings me to another rationale of the Government in this so-called tax reform. It says that tax reform will make us more competitive with the United States. I must question that. The United States has an estate tax which Canada has not had since 1971. Furthermore, we as Canadians value what makes us a distinct society. We value safer streets. We value a publicly financed hospital and health care system. Indeed, it was the NDP and CCF, with J. S. Woodsworth and Tommy Douglas, that pioneered these health care programs. We value a greater public role in the area of financing of post-secondary education, in transportation, and in communications. Canadians are prepared to pay the cost if our tax system is fair.
The Government's argument that we must lower these rates to bring them more in line with American rates is part and parcel with its approach to Canadian society, which is best exemplified in the trade deal. That deal, if it is ultimately implemented, will result in Canada in many ways being transformed into something like a fifty-first state. It will erode our social programs and destroy our sovereignty, resulting in far greater levels of unemployment. We as New Democrats are pledged to fight that deal with every ounce of energy we have.
Another rationale of the Government is that the upper level of taxation should be reduced because no one pays at those upper levels in any event. If that is the case, surely those loopholes should be closed. Rather than lower the upper marginal rate, close the loopholes that allow people who are making in excess of $100,000 to pay no income tax whatsoever. That is a more sensible approach than simply lowering the upper level of taxation.
Another argument made by the Government is that higher tax rates breed inefficiency. Japan is often cited as one of the most productive economies in the world. It has a top tax rate of 80 per cent. Sweden, which has a very high growth economy, has a top rate of 88 per cent. Studies have shown that high tax rates have little effect on productivity.
In bringing this proposal forward, the Government still has not moved to implement a minimum tax on its friends in the corporate sector. Even Ronald Reagan has taken such steps in the United States, and in excess of $2 billion in revenue has
been raised as a result of the minithum tax on the corporate sector there.
The New Democratic Party agrees that loopholes were opened by the Liberals during their term in office. We would have hoped that the Tories would have closed those loopholes and moved to a fair, just and equitable tax system. This tax reform is nothing of the sort. That is why in the next election Canadians will turn not to the Liberals, not to the Conservatives, but to New Democrats for a tax system which is fair and equitable.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's heart is in the right place. He is right when he says there is something immoral about our society when we see Canadian children w'ho come home at the end of the day and have to go to bed hungry and who get up in the morning and go to school hungry. These problems are caused by poverty, and it is true that they are a blot on this wealthy society of ours. However, the answer is not tax reform but a family policy that will help these children. These problems are caused by the lack of a comprehensive family policy that would include a housing policy, providing decent, affordable housing SO that at the end of the month, parents would not be in a situation where they don't have enough money to make ends meet and give their children the food they need.
On the other hand, since the Hon. Member mentioned that the sales tax is a regressive tax, I would like to point out to him that we felt that a tax reform was necessary because we had reached the point where the only way we could get the money to upgrade programs to help the poor was to increase sales tax, because we could no longer increase personal income tax.
The tax burden on Canadians was undermining job creation, so a tax reform was necessary but we also had to make sure that we could get revenue from sources other than sales tax. These are the two aspects of the reform: income tax and sales tax.
As far as sales tax is concerned, we have introduced a credit to compensate people at the bottom of the financial ladder, a $50 credit for all Canadians. So an effort has been made, but the tax reform must be carried out. The Hon. Member may not agree on ideological issues or on the procedure, but our purpose, Mr. Speaker, is to provide some relief for Canadians who are overtaxed, and we want to do so by finding sources of revenue so that the Government can upgrade programs that deal with the problems of the poor, whether they are children, adults, or senior citizens. Sixty percent of the women over 65 in Canada are poor. So would he not agree that something had to be done and that we are taking this approach for a very good reason? And as far as capital gains are concerned, this also covers farmers, who are not wealthy people. I don't think he should blame tax reform for the problems caused by poverty which have been with us for quite some time.
July 20, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I find the Member's observation absolutely unbelievable. First of all, she does admit that the sales tax is regressive, does she not? So if it is a regressive tax, as the Member says, why have the Conservatives increased the level of that sales tax since 1984? Why, Mr. Speaker, have they increased the sales tax twice, if it is a regressive tax? The Members admits that, Mr. Speaker, and I find it unbelievable that she now says that there is no another way of obtaining the necessary money. There is another way, and it's quite plain to see. Why have they not taxed corporations, in the interest of fairness? Why, Mr. Speaker, have they not taxed corporations instead of increasing the sales tax every year? That is what I do not understand.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has in fact removed $3.1 billion from the tax system. The 2 per cent of Canadians with the highest incomes will receive $379 million, but the 26 per cent who are among the poorest of Canadians will only receive $257 million. And there you have Conservative tax reform!
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Members ask me why we must use the tax system to reduce poverty. We New Democrats believe that the tax system can be used in a fair way to finance social programs, for instance, programs to help poor children, the homeless, and the elderly who are grappling with poverty. We think we can use the tax system and the money obtained by way of it to improve our social programs in a fair way. The Conservatives will not recognize that reality, and instead they help their friends in the corporate sector, in the corporate elite, and because of that the Canadian tax system remains unfair.

Mr. Speaker, when I saw the Flon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) rise in that beautiful red Liberal tie, I thought he was at least going to say some kind things about the Liberals. However, he began by indicating that the next Government would be a New Democratic Government. In the light of that, I think it is worth taking seriously the proposals he said would be part of New Democratic tax reform.
He indicated that capital gains would be taxed at full rates. This, of course, is tragic news for many senior citizens whose savings include Bell Canada stock which they have held for 20 and 30 years in some cases and will all be taxed in one year.
Conrad Black's parents?

I wanted to ask the Member about the small business and family farm exemption. Under the New Democratic tax system, he said, that although capital gains would be taxed fully the family farm, and small business and the family-owned business, would not be taxed at the regular capital gains rates which the NDP would impose. 1 think it is important, if those Members are proposing that a New Democratic Government be created in the next election, for us to know exactly what these exemptions are.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
After all, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) referred to his great friends, Conrad Black and family. Perhaps Argus Corporation is a family company in the definition of the New Democrats, or some of the largest farms in the country owned by one family. Are they to be totally exempt from capital gains tax under a New Democratic Government?
In a nutshell I am asking for more details about the exemption which will apply to family farms and to small family-owned businesses under New Democratic tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that a Liberal front-bencher should rise and be somewhat sensitive in the area of tax reform, particularly someone who has been around since 1968. It was the Liberal Government that was responsible for introducing loopholes into the tax system in this country that resulted in the loss of billions of dollars in tax revenue.
Some of us remember the scientific tax credit. Some of those Members will remember the research tax credit. Those great managers of the economy brought forward this boondoggle that resulted in the loss of literally billions of dollars. It is not surprising that the Member from one of the York constituencies would rise and raise concerns.
The reality is that when we look at the question of capital gains exemptions we must look at who in fact benefits most from these exemptions. I have made it very clear that the exemption for the family farm and for small businesses will continue, but let us look at who it is that benefits from capital gains. In 1984, the 1 per cent of taxpayers with incomes above $100,000 received 34 per cent of all capital gains. It is not surprising that the Liberals should be defending those people because in fact some of them, until a couple of years ago, used to be their principal source of funds, although the Liberals are now having some difficulty in collecting these funds.
I think it is interesting as well to note that on July 1 of this year the Chief Electoral Officer published the statement of the source of revenue of the three political Parties in Canada. As New Democrats, we are proud that we are a democratically financed Party, financed by the people of Canada. The Liberal Party and the Conservative Party receive thousands and thousands of dollars from the banks. The Liberal Party receives something like $50,000 a year from the banks. The Conservatives receive $50,000 a year from each of the major banks in the country.
It is not surprising that the Liberals are somewhat sensitive. They have a record of fiscal incompetence that is embarrassing. Canadians will never again allow them anywhere near the reins of power. They will go the way of the Liberal Party of the United Kingdom and the way of the dodo bird. They will be relics of the past.

Hear, hear!

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts

Mr. Speaker, it is rich listening to the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) talking about the funding and financing of the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party and contrasting it to the democratic methods by which funds are raised by his Party. Yet the New Democratic Party is the only Party in the country which had a contributor go to the Federal Court of Canada to try to get his contribution back. He got it back, too. He did not want to contribute to the New Democratic Party. The banks which have made contributions to other Parties, as other companies have done, have at least done it voluntarily. New Democratic contributors want their money back. The court is ready to give it back to them. I do not think that the New Democratic Party should be telling Liberals and Conservatives anything about democratic fund-raising.
I have another question for the Hon. Member for Burnaby. It does not matter much that I do not get to ask it and have an answer from him, since I did not get an answer to the last question I asked. I asked him how he would define small business. He was unable but, more likely, he was unwilling to define small business for the purpose of the New Democratic capital gains tax exemption. I would be very interested to hear him-and I challenge him on some early occasion, or any other member of his Party-give the Canadian people more details about the exemptions that will be available from their Government in the unlikely opportunity, but the possibility, that they form the Government after the next election.
I have another question that I wanted to ask him, and since I did not get much of an answer to the last one, I think I will ask this one anyway as a hypothetical question. He indicated that following the next election in spite of the polls and in spite of what all of us who travel across the country meeting voters know if there is not a New Democratic Government, what his advice would be to people who are in the following situation. They cannot vote for the New Democratic Party. They might have been beguiled by what the Hon. Member had to say about tax reform, but they do not feel that they can support a political Party that wants to take Canada out of NATO. They do not feel that they can support a political Party that wants to nationalize at least one of the banks. They do not want to see the Government running a bank in addition to all the other things that Governments run and perhaps should not. Maybe they will say that they do not want to vote for a Party whose justice critic voted against the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Let us say that we were dealing with a voter who could not support with good reasons the New Democratic Party. Would he advise on the basis of taxation that that voter vote for the Liberals or the Conservatives? I do not know what the Hon. Member would have said if I had called on him, but I believe that he would have said, and that his advice to the Canadian people would be, to vote Liberal in a case like that. That is why I thought he was wearing a red tie.
There are some things that should be said about this tax reform package presented by the Government. I want to try to say some of them right now. The first thing that has to be said is that this is not tax reform. I remember during the last Parliament watching some very sincere activities by Members
opposite, members of the Conservative Opposition in those days, directed toward improving the taxation system. I remember the efforts of the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) to try to make the tax system simpler and less complicated. I think of how ironic it is that a political Party that in opposition developed a plan for making the taxation system simpler should have produced what it calls tax reform which is so much more complicated.
In my constituency office last Saturday afternoon I had a line-up of people who needed help with this long blue form that they had all received to enter into the simplified tax reform. It is not hard to do your twelfth, thirteenth or fourteenth form. But it is very complicated for the average individual to sit and look through and answer the complicated questions by which this so-called tax reform is being launched. It is not simpler. It is more complicated.
Also on the subject of tax reform, I remember in the last Parliament the efforts of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to try to deal frankly, openly, and honestly with taxation issues. I think he was very sincere when he was doing that. What I find to be the most astonishing feature of this so-called tax reform is the misrepresentations that it contains, the blatant efforts to pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian people about what is happening in this so-called tax reform. I do not think Canadians will be fooled by this.
When the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) stood up and said that four out of Five Canadians would find their taxes reduced by tax reform, he knew the full story. What he meant by that statement was that four out of five Canadians would pay less tax under this tax reform than they did in the immediately preceding year, which was the third year of Conservative Government.
What he did not say and what he is hoping the Canadian people will not find out is that those four out of five taxpayers have had substantial tax increases under this Government, so much so that the reduction in this tax reform is no reduction at all. Each of those people, if they are in the same income level that they were when this Government took office, will be paying substantially more taxes as a result of a Conservative Government than they would have without any of these tax measures over the last four years.
I say that it is a misrepresentation to stand up and say that four out of five Canadians will pay less taxes this year than last. It is true, but when we look at the whole picture we see a Government that has engaged in what our Leader has called, and quite truly, the largest tax grab in the history of Canada.
I would like to say something very direct and blunt about tax increases because when the Hon. Member stood up, and I asked him a question about it, he said: "Oh yes, but we had a big deficit to pay off which we inherited from the former Government". It is true, there was a big deficit built up during the Liberal years of office. A great many good things were done with that money. In retrospect one can see that we should
July 20, 1988

have paid our way more as we went along. I concede that there was a big deficit. In years of prosperity something should be done to reduce the deficit. I am not arguing about that. I am not saying that taxes should never be increased. I am not saying that this Government should not have had to increase taxes. 1 am not saying that a Liberal Government, if there had been one in office, would not have increased taxes. 1 say something that I believe to the bottom of my heart: a Liberal Government would never increase taxes in a way which makes poor and middle-income people pay more while the richest people, the highest income earners in society, pay less. Their taxes go down while lower and middle-income Canadians have their taxes increased. I would like to think when Liberals have to increase taxes that they would be increased on a progressive basis, in order that those best able to pay would be the ones who would pay more, not those who are most able to pay would pay less. That is the formula followed by the Conservative Government.
The Minister of Finance had a cute phrase: "We want more wealthy people in Canada". That is an interesting idea. It is a good idea. If there are more wealthy people in the country, it is not a bad thing, but if people are made wealthy by having their taxes lowered while the deficit accumulated on the books is approached by making poor and middle income people pay more, that is fraud. It is not liberalism, and it is not tax reform. I hope the Canadian people will see through what this Government has done and call a spade a spade.
Another thing that astonishes me coming from the lips of the Minister of Finance, who was very sincere and dedicated while in opposition to have genuine tax reform, was the Government stating that tax reform has removed 850,000 lower income persons from having to pay income tax.
That's right.

"That's right", the Member opposite says. This year, without tax reform, 850,000 more people would have had to pay taxes than would have paid them without this so-called tax reform. Like the four out of five Canadians who are supposed to be better off, I would like to look at the situation of the 850,000 lower-income persons who have been removed from the tax rolls. Who are they? Did they suddenly get jobs and that is why they are having to pay taxes or not having to pay taxes? Those 850,000 people are the poorest Canadians who, in spite of their poverty and low incomes, were added to the tax rolls by measures the Conservative Government introduced since it came to office. There is no doubt about that.
The Fraser Institute has laid it out chapter and verse. In the first year of office the Government eliminated the inflation adjustment for taxes. The former Government had a policy that raised the floor in order that low-incomc Canadians were not brought into the tax rolls just because of inflation. That was introduced by the Leader of our Party when he was Minister of Finance. For a decade of Liberal Government
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
every year the floor on income taxes increased so that poor people, who were not paying taxes the year before because of inflation, would not find that they were obliged to pay taxes because their inflated incomes brought them into the tax roll.
This hard-hearted, cruel, oriented to the rich, regressive Government removed that adjustment so that poor people, because of inflation and not because their real incomes went up, came into the tax roll year after year of Conservative Government. Over one million people became income taxpayers because of that change in income taxation. They became taxpayers not because they benefited from prosperity during a Conservative Government, which is what the Minister of Finance tried to say-

Maybe they got a job. Did you ever supply
any?

I am not talking about those people. I am talking about people whose real incomes did not change. Some people did get jobs. Many jobs have been created during the last few years in Canada, in the United States, and in every industrialized country, but additional taxpayers appeared in Canada because of the callous policies of the Government introduced in its first years in office. According to the Fraser Institute over one million people became taxpayers because of inflation, although their real incomes did not change.
Now we get the great news that 850,000 of those one million people are being put back, as far as taxation is concerned, to where they were when the Liberals were in office. That is the Government's idea of tax reform. It might be the Government's idea of tax reform. When it says to those 850,000 people who would otherwise have had to pay taxes that under Tory taxation they will no longer do so, perhaps some people will think that a break is being given to lower-income Canadians, but the Government is not even restoring the situation that Canadians faced before the last election. There are still 150,000 people whose real incomes have not increased and who are paying taxes thanks to the Tories. During the election campaign we will see how grateful they are.
I am also concerned about child care. There is something in this wonderful tax reform package for mothers. What has been put on the table by the Government is so far from what is needed and so far from what it promised in the last election campaign that to call it tax reform and put it forward as a reason for voting Tory in the next election is the most bizarre proposition that has ever been put forward.
"We cannot afford it", the Hon. Member says, as he turns his back and marches out of the House. Canadians said the same thing about the old age pension. They said the same thing about medicare. They said the same thing about our massive support for post-secondary education, that we could not afford those things. Justice requires that Canada develop on an urgent basis an adequate child care program. Not only that, the economy demands it.

July 20, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
While we were bringing into place other major social reforms in this country, some of which I have just described, we were not focusing too much on child care. We lived with a reality, which has now become a myth, that there is a spouse at home looking after the children. When we needed to face up to old age pensions, and when we needed to face up to medicare and so on, child care was not competing because there was a spouse at home looking after the children and child care seemed like a frill.
All three political Parties officially recognize the reality; it was recognized in the last election campaign. There is no spouse at home dedicating herself or himself full time to looking after the house and children. She is at work, or she is loqking for a job, or she has a job. She is not working for extra money to supplement the family income. In many cases-less than half, but perhaps in my riding more than most-such a woman is the sole income earner for a family with children. There is no adequate child care system.
The Government proposed a child care system. I did an analysis of it with the 200,000 additional day care spaces that were going to be created. One-tenth of the entire national production of this government program is needed in my riding. The City of North York in Metropolitan Toronto is 20,000 day care spaces short. There are more than 10 ridings in Canada; in fact there are nearly 300. We cannot say that we cannot afford it and return to that old rhetoric. We are talking about a program which is an economic reform and a way of taking a burden off the minds of mothers in my riding who need to work to support their families and cannot find a proper place for their children to be cared for during the day.
I do not like to hear men saying that a proper child care program is a frill, that it is not necessary, that it is too expensive, because unlike the other programs I mentioned child care is one where the injustice is borne by and large by women.
In this place where the majority of Members of Parliament are men, we have to be extra sensitive to a woman's point of view. I do not think Hon. Members are sensitive when they say that child care is a fringe or a frill that we cannot afford to have right now. We need to do justice to the mothers of this country by having an adequate child care program.
Right on.

What is in the tax reform? The tax reform contains a couple of hundred dollars per child for each mother.
When Members opposite were asked about this program over the months that they were trying to bamboozle Canadians into considering their child care package to be worth while, they said: "Well, it is up to the mother. If she wants to spend it on her children, if she wants to establish child care, she has the money and she can do what she likes".
We on this side of the House know that that attitude will not create a national child care program in Canada. We do not want it totally in the public sector. We do not want to nationalize the kinds of child care facilities that there are across this country. Many of them are adequate. Many of them are economical. Many of them provide employment for mothers who take in four or five other children from their apartment building to look after them during the day. We do not want, as the New Democratic Party does, to see those types of day care facilities expropriated by the Government in favour of public child care. We have put forward a program. We want an honest, acceptable, comprehensive child care program that will give the women of this country justice. By the way, it will give the children of this country a good start in life, with a proper child care system containing great standards. This tax reform fails on every count. It should be rejected by us in this House, and it should be rejected by the Canadian people in the next election.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville.

Mr. Speaker, I know that in a certain context the word "hypocrisy" is unparliamentary, but sometimes one has difficulty in this House understanding what is meant by that word. Perhaps the Hon. Member could help me with its definition. I wonder if this would correspond to an acceptable definition of hypocrisy: the notion that somehow it is illegitimate for a democratically elected union to determine democratically that contributions will be made to the New Democratic Party, being criticized for such but at the same time being perfectly acceptable for $80,000 in money from depositors and shareholders in banks to be contributed to the Liberal Party, even though individual depositors and individual shareholders may object to it. I wonder if seeing a difference between those two is not hypocrisy.
The Liberal Party criticizes the inadequacies of the Progressive Conservative Government with respect to tax reform which it could have brought about in the many years that it was in power. Is that not hypocrisy? I wonder if there is not a danger of hypocrisy in the notion proposed by a certain Leader of the Liberal Party that there would be no wage and price controls and subsequently introduce such wage and price controls, and whether that kind of hypocrisy does not hint at the kind of hypocrisy that one might expect in the same Party with respect to free trade. It is a Party that said that it will tear it up, but a Party that also had great difficulty, recently, in getting contributions from those same banks, large corporations, and corporate people in respect to their fund-raising. I do not know what hypocrisy is, but I wonder if the members of the Liberal Party could not give us a better definition of it, by virtue of experience, than anybody else in the House.
July 20, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I think that when I am finished perhaps the Hon. Member will have a better understanding, because 1 want to put it precisely in the context of the questions that he asked. I criticized the New Democratic Party because it attacked our method of fund-raising to get contributions from banks, from virtually anyone who wants to contribute, wlple in the New Democratic Party I mentioned that someone went to the Federal Court of Canada to get his money back. They belonged to a union. As the Member said, they democratically decided that they were going to support the union and therefore every member, whether he liked it or not, had to contribute.
The Member asked me: "How is that different from a bank? Do the shareholders and the depositors get a say in whether the contribution is made?" As a matter of fact they do not. If an individual shareholder finds that the directors of the bank have decided to make a contribution to the Conservative Party and to the Liberal Party, and he may not like it. there is nothing he can do about it. If a depositor who is depositing in a bank learns that the bank is spending part of its money by making contributions to the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party, he cannot change the bank's policy. There is a very important difference in a contribution that the union makes and a contribution that a bank makes. If I do not want my bank to contribute to the Conservative Party or to the Liberal Party, I can move my money to another bank. If I am a depositor and I am not happy with the bank's investment, policy, I can take my money out.
Which other bank?

If I am a shareholder and I, find out that the Bank of Nova Scotia is contributing to the Liberal Party and I do not like it, I can sell my shares and buy shares in another bank. This unionist is forced to pay dues to the union, whether he likes it or not and whether he joins or not and he is forced to see part of his dues go to the New Democratic Party.
An Hon. iMember: The shareholder in the bank has no choice at all.

The unionist can leave his job.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts

Yes, the unionist can leave his job and the shareholder of a bank can sell his stock. There is not much of a parallel in saying that you can sell your shares and invest in another bank that contributes to the political Party that you like, I suppose there are co-operative banks registered as such that make contributions to the New Democratic Party. If someone is unhappy with the way that they are handled as a depositor and with what happens with their money, they can change.
Do you know what you have to do to get relief if you are a member of a union or if you are paying dues to a union? There is no stock to sell. There are no deposits to transfer. You have to do what someone recently did; you have to go to court. He had to go to the Federal Court of Canada to get back the money that the union contributed out of his dues, against his will, to the New Democratic Party. What is hypocrisy? I think it is failing to recognize that.
I wanted to, take some time to also talk about loopholes. The Liberal Government introduced a lot of loopholes, which were characterized as tax incentives and designed to produce certain results. I a,m not saying that they all worked. Why the Conservatives did not stop the science endeavour when they should have, why they let it run on and on for a billion dollars, I do not know, but tax loopholes created certain important industries in this country such as the movie industry. I do not think that we want to do without it. A loophole was meant to be an incentive. In many cases, they were incentives. If they were exceeded, as the Members opposite said, they should have changed them and stopped them when they first took office.
They shouldn't have even got in.

They should not have gotten in. I agree with that.
